title: Teach dramatic irony through a line
statement: Teach dramatic irony through a line the audience hears and the deceived character does not, keeping what the audience knows apart from what each character knows.
detail: The handover's opening introduces the audience's knowledge of the deceiver's lies while keeping apart what the audience knows and what the hero knows, and its fifth scene sets the deceiver's private line against his public name before defining the term, with a factual check after. A later review asked for the definition to come with an example, and the film added a step between the quote and the definition saying the hero never hears the line while the audience does. The recorded script makes the same move in speech just before it defines the term.

evidence.quote: It introduces the audience’s knowledge of Iago’s deceit while preserving the distinction between what the audience knows and what Othello knows.
5. What Iago says. Contrast “I am not what I am” with “Honest Iago” and define dramatic irony. A factual check follows.
Define with an example: we hear "I am not what I am", Othello does not
a step between the quote and the definition: "Othello never hears it · We do"
Othello never hears this. We do. That is dramatic irony: the audience knows something a character doesn’t.
